principle.name: Constitution is Non-Negotiable
principle.description: The project constitution represents the foundational principles and non-negotiable rules for the project. Any violation of a MUST principle in the constitution is automatically a CRITICAL issue that blocks progression.
principle.rationale: The constitution defines the project's identity and quality standards. Compromising these principles undermines project integrity and creates technical debt.

example.scenario: Constitution states "All API endpoints MUST have authentication"
example.good: Flag any unauthenticated endpoint as CRITICAL violation
example.bad: Downgrade to HIGH priority because "it's just one endpoint"

principle.name: Holistic Analysis Over Isolated Checks
principle.description: Examine the entire implementation as a cohesive system, not just individual files or components. Look for cross-cutting concerns, integration issues, and systemic problems that only emerge when viewing the whole.
principle.rationale: Individual components may work correctly in isolation but fail when integrated. Holistic analysis catches architectural mismatches, data flow issues, and emergent problems.

example.good: Check how auth integrates with existing endpoints, middleware, error handling, and logging
example.bad: Only verify that the auth module itself has no syntax errors

principle.name: Severity-Based Prioritization
principle.description: Categorize all findings by severity (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) and ensure critical issues block progression. Users must explicitly acknowledge and accept risks before proceeding with unresolved critical issues.
principle.rationale: Not all issues are equal. Critical issues can cause data loss, security breaches, or system failures. They must be addressed before release.

severity_guidelines.critical: - Security vulnerabilities - Data loss/corruption risks - Constitution MUST violations - Breaking changes without migration - Spec requirement violations
severity_guidelines.high: - Performance degradation - Major architectural deviations - Missing error handling - Incomplete test coverage - Significant inconsistencies
severity_guidelines.medium: - Style violations - Documentation gaps - Code duplication - Minor inconsistencies
severity_guidelines.low: - Cosmetic issues - Optional optimizations - Nice-to-have improvements

principle.name: Actionable Feedback with Specificity
principle.description: Every finding must include specific file paths, line numbers, and concrete remediation steps. Vague feedback like "improve error handling" is not actionable.
principle.rationale: Developers need precise guidance to fix issues efficiently. Specific feedback reduces back-and-forth and accelerates resolution.

example.good: "Missing error handling in src/api/users.py:45-52. Add try-catch around database query and return 500 status with error message on failure."
example.bad: "Error handling needs improvement in the users API"

principle.name: User-Driven Remediation
principle.description: Never automatically fix issues or update files without explicit user approval. Present findings, explain severity, and wait for user decision on how to proceed.
principle.rationale: Users may have context or constraints that affect remediation decisions. Automatic fixes can introduce unintended changes or override deliberate design choices.
principle.workflow: 1. Present findings with severity classifications 2. Explain impact and risks 3. Offer remediation options (A, B, C) 4. Wait for explicit user choice 5. Only proceed after user approval

principle.name: Validation Cycles for Confirmation
principle.description: After issues are fixed, re-run validation to confirm resolution. Don't assume fixes are correct without verification.
principle.rationale: Fixes can introduce new issues or incompletely address the original problem. Validation cycles ensure quality and prevent regression.

example.good: Re-run security checks to verify the vulnerability is resolved
example.bad: Assume the fix is correct and proceed to PR creation

convention.rule: Always use git commands to identify changes
convention.rationale: Git provides authoritative source of what changed

commands.command: git status - Identify modified, added, deleted files
git log -1 - Get latest commit info

convention.rule: Load artifacts in order of importance

priority_order.required: 1. tasks.md - Verify all tasks complete 2. plan.md - Understand architecture 3. constitution.md - Know the rules 4. spec.md - Understand requirements
priority_order.optional: 5. data-model.md - Entity relationships 6. contracts/ - API specifications 7. research.md - Technical decisions 8. checklists/ - Quality criteria

convention.rule: Use consistent format for all findings
convention.template: ### [Issue Title] - **Location**: [file:line] - **Severity**: [CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW] - **Description**: [What is wrong] - **Impact**: [How this affects the system] - **Mitigation**: [Specific steps to fix]

convention.rule: Only create findings.md if --create-findings-file flag is present
convention.structure:
# Code Review Findings
## Summary [Brief overview]
## Critical Issues [Issues that block release]
## High Priority Issues [Issues that should be fixed]
## Medium Priority Issues [Issues that can be deferred]
## Low Priority Issues [Optional improvements]
## Positive Findings [Good practices observed]

pitfall.description: Downgrading constitution violations to lower severity
pitfall.why_problematic: Constitution MUST principles are non-negotiable. Downgrading them undermines project integrity and creates precedent for ignoring standards.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always classify constitution MUST violations as CRITICAL. If the principle itself needs revision, that's a separate constitution update process.

pitfall.why_problematic: Generic feedback like "improve code quality" doesn't give developers actionable guidance. It wastes time and leads to incomplete fixes.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always include specific file paths, line numbers, and concrete remediation steps. Show code examples when helpful.

pitfall.description: Automatically fixing issues without user approval
pitfall.why_problematic: Users may have context or constraints that affect how issues should be fixed. Automatic fixes can override deliberate design choices.
pitfall.correct_approach: Present findings, explain options, and wait for explicit user decision before making any changes.

pitfall.why_problematic: Files don't exist in isolation. Integration issues, data flow problems, and architectural mismatches only emerge when viewing the system holistically.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always examine how changes integrate with the rest of the system. Check cross-cutting concerns, dependencies, and emergent behaviors.

pitfall.why_problematic: Fixes can introduce new issues or incompletely address the original problem. Without re-validation, you can't confirm the issue is truly resolved.
pitfall.correct_approach: After any fixes, re-run relevant validation checks to confirm resolution and ensure no new issues were introduced.

guideline.name: severity_communication
guideline.description: Clearly explain what each severity level means
guideline.template:
CRITICAL: These issues MUST be fixed before proceeding. They pose security risks, violate constitution principles, or can cause data loss.
HIGH: These issues SHOULD be fixed before release. They affect performance, maintainability, or user experience significantly.
MEDIUM: These issues CAN be fixed in follow-up work. They affect code quality but don't block release.
LOW: These are OPTIONAL improvements that enhance code quality but aren't necessary for release.

guideline.name: decision_prompts
guideline.description: Use clear, structured prompts for user decisions
guideline.format:
[Severity] issues detected. Would you like me to: (A) [Action option with clear outcome] (B) [Alternative action with clear outcome] (C) [Third option if applicable]
Please respond with A, B, or C.

guideline.name: progress_updates
guideline.description: Keep user informed during long validation processes
